body:
## Why

`hkb link 288 304` reads in English as "288 depends on 304". It means the reverse: it made **#304 blocked
by #288**. Hit for real on 2026-09-03 re-sequencing root A behind #304; the only signal was the output
line, and the fix was `unlink 288 304` then `link 304 288`.

The help says `link <parent> <child>`, which is correct and is no help at the moment of typing: "parent"
and "child" do not say which one waits. Every *other* place the same relation is expressed says it the
other way round — `hkb create "x" --blocked-by 41` puts the waiting card first, and `hkb list` renders it
`#288 ⇐ #304`, arrow pointing at the blocker. So the CLI has two orders for one relation and the rarer one
is the positional command.

An operator recovers from this in two commands. A worker following the protocol may not notice at all: a
wrong edge does not error, it just makes a card unreachable or ready too early, which is the silent-failure
class (value 5).

## What

1. `hkb link` and `unlink` take the same order as everything else: `hkb link <card> --blocked-by <blocker>`,
   with the bare two-positional form kept and **printed back in the `⇐` notation** so the direction is
   visible without reading the docs: `#288 ⇐ #304 (linked)`.
2. Refuse the obvious mistake: linking a card to one that already blocks it in the other direction is a
   cycle — `hkb link` should say so rather than create it. (Check whether `computeReady` already survives a
   cycle; if it does, this is still worth refusing at the verb.)
3. `hkb help` names the relation in words on the same line: "link <parent> <child> — the child must finish
   before the parent can start".

## Done when

- [ ] The `--blocked-by` form works and is what `hkb help` shows first.
- [ ] Both forms print the resulting edge in `⇐` notation.
- [ ] A cycle is refused with exit 2 naming both cards.
- [ ] Tests for the order, the echo, and the cycle refusal.
- [ ] `npm run lint && npm test` green.
title: hkb link <a> <b> reads as "a depends on b" and means the opposite, with nothing to confirm the direction
